wholeLesson.title: Anticipate Potassium, Sodium, and Volume Effects
wholeLesson.summary: Trimethoprim has an amiloride-like effect on distal sodium entry, reducing potassium secretion. High doses can also produce natriuresis and hyponatremia. Kidney dysfunction and interacting drugs magnify risk.
wholeLesson.application: Create a laboratory plan with baseline and early repeat potassium, sodium, creatinine, dose, renal function, interacting drugs, symptoms, and an explicit response threshold.

lesson.heading: Connect the distal sodium effect to potassium retention
lesson.body: Trimethoprim has an amiloride-like action at sodium channels in the distal nephron. Reduced sodium entry lowers the electrical driving force for potassium secretion, so potassium can accumulate. This renal effect is separate from the antibacterial folate mechanism. It explains why a familiar antibiotic can interact with kidney function and potassium-raising medicines even when the infection is responding.

lesson.heading: Potassium risk is cumulative
lesson.body: Review kidney function, baseline potassium, age, trimethoprim exposure and the complete medication list before treatment. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, other potassium-sparing medicines, potassium supplements and salt substitutes can add to impaired potassium excretion. High exposure increases concern, but the BACTRIM label also warns that recommended doses can cause hyperkalemia in patients with renal insufficiency, potassium-handling disorders or interacting medicines. A routine course is not a reason to omit follow-up.

lesson.heading: High-dose therapy can waste sodium
lesson.body: Trimethoprim-related sodium loss can contribute to hyponatremia and volume depletion, particularly during high-dose therapy such as treatment for Pneumocystis pneumonia. A low sodium result alone does not identify the mechanism. Review the sodium trend, symptoms, dose, kidney function, diuretics, intake and volume status. Consider a salt-losing drug effect rather than automatically diagnosing SIADH; neither mechanism should be assumed solely from the medication name. Symptomatic hyponatremia requires prompt evaluation and appropriate correction.

lesson.heading: Monitoring must occur while harm is preventable
lesson.body: Obtain baseline potassium, sodium and kidney information, then arrange follow-up during treatment according to the dose, risk, duration, symptoms and renal trajectory. A normal baseline does not establish safety for the entire course. The current BACTRIM label calls for close potassium monitoring in patients at risk and ongoing clinical chemistry, urinalysis and renal assessment, particularly with impaired renal function. Name the repeat-testing date, who reviews the result and how an abnormal result changes the plan. Reassess when exposure or kidney function changes rather than waiting automatically for the final dose.

lesson.heading: Hydration is individualized
lesson.body: The review book advises water with sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim because urinary crystals can occur. Current BACTRIM labeling calls for adequate fluid intake and urine output to prevent crystalluria. Assess intake, output, kidney function and volume status when making that advice executable. Retain an individualized plan for a patient with heart failure, congestion or limited kidney reserve; a universal large fluid load does not account for those constraints. Drinking more water also does not replace potassium, sodium or renal monitoring.

lesson.heading: Act on significant abnormalities and reassess the antibiotic
lesson.body: Monitoring must lead to a decision. Current BACTRIM labeling directs discontinuation when a significant electrolyte abnormality or renal insufficiency is detected. Review the result and symptoms promptly, assess the clinical urgency and address the abnormality with appropriate care. Reassess the indication, susceptibility, dose, renal exposure and whether an effective alternative is available. A safer substitute still needs to treat the original infection. Document the responsible clinician, communication and follow-up so that an abnormal result does not become an unattended laboratory value.

keyPoints: TMP can reduce distal potassium secretion.

check.question: With comparable TMP-SMX exposure, which patient has the strongest combination of kidney and medication risks for hyperkalemia?
choices: A patient with CKD taking lisinopril and spironolactone
A patient with normal kidney function and no potassium-raising medicines
A patient with normal kidney function taking amlodipine and no potassium products
A patient with normal kidney function taking an ARB alone and no other potassium-raising medicine
check.rationale: Kidney impairment, lisinopril and spironolactone combine risks for potassium retention when TMP-SMX is considered. Review the indication and alternatives, baseline potassium and renal function, and arrange follow-up with a named reviewer. Recommended antibiotic doses do not remove the interaction risk. Significant electrolyte abnormalities require action under the current product instructions.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: Which renal effect explains trimethoprim-associated hyperkalemia?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Trimethoprim can reduce distal potassium secretion through an amiloride-like effect
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Matches the observed distal sodium-channel/potassium-secretion mechanism.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Trimethoprim directly increases distal potassium secretion
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Reverses the potassium-secretion effect.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Hyperkalemia occurs only when the infecting organism is resistant
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Confuses infection susceptibility with the renal drug effect.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Recommended antibiotic doses prevent any effect on renal potassium handling
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Contradicts labeled risk at recommended doses.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: The amiloride-like distal sodium-channel effect reduces potassium secretion. This is a renal drug effect rather than evidence of bacterial resistance. The current label warns that susceptible patients can develop hyperkalemia even at recommended doses.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: Which clinical action best manages TMP-SMX potassium risk in a high-risk patient?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Check potassium early in high-risk patients and change therapy when risk is unacceptable
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Testing during exposure and changing an unsafe plan addresses the retained potassium risk.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Measure potassium only after the antibiotic course ends
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Postpones detection until after exposure.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Keep treatment unchanged despite a significant potassium abnormality
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Ignores the label action for a significant abnormality.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Add a potassium supplement routinely to counter the antibiotic effect
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Adds potassium to a potassium-retention problem without an indication.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: Plan potassium follow-up while the patient is receiving treatment, review kidney function and interacting medicines, and act on significant abnormalities. Waiting until the final dose, continuing through a significant abnormality or adding potassium does not address potassium-retention risk.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: Which assessment best addresses TMP-SMX-associated hyperkalemia risk?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Assess baseline potassium, kidney function, dose, ACE inhibitor, ARB, MRA, potassium products, and follow-up time
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Includes potassium, renal exposure, interacting products and follow-up.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Use the prescribed tablet strength alone to determine potassium safety
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Strength alone cannot determine patient potassium safety.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Review creatinine but omit baseline potassium and potassium-raising medicines
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Omits potassium and interacting medicines.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Confirm a normal baseline potassium and omit any follow-up plan
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: One normal baseline does not cover subsequent exposure.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: Potassium risk reflects the result, kidney function, dose and combined medicines or products. A tablet name, creatinine alone or one normal baseline cannot replace the full assessment and a timed follow-up plan.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: Which monitoring error is most important to prevent in a high-risk TMP-SMX potassium combination?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Waiting until the end of therapy to monitor a high-risk combination
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Defers surveillance beyond the period when harm may develop.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Reviewing kidney function and baseline potassium before treatment
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Appropriate baseline kidney/potassium assessment.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Arranging repeat potassium during the antibiotic course
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Appropriate repeat assessment during exposure.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Assigning a clinician to review and act on follow-up results
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Appropriate ownership of interpretation and action.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: The error is postponing surveillance until treatment is finished. Risk assessment, testing during exposure and clear review ownership help detect harm while the plan can still be changed.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: Which principle best explains a possible sodium effect during high-dose trimethoprim therapy?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: High-dose trimethoprim can promote natriuresis and clinically important hyponatremia
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Compatible with sodium transport findings and high-dose cohort/case observations.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Every low sodium result during TMP-SMX proves SIADH
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: One low sodium result does not prove SIADH.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Trimethoprim cannot affect sodium excretion because it is an antibiotic
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Antibacterial use does not exclude a renal transport effect.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Higher trimethoprim exposure guarantees that serum sodium stays normal
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: High dose does not guarantee sodium safety.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: Primary transport evidence and clinical observations support a sodium-losing effect, and the label warns about serious hyponatremia. A low sodium result still requires a clinical assessment; neither SIADH nor a trimethoprim salt-losing mechanism follows from the drug name alone.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: Which clinical action best addresses sodium risk during high-intensity TMP-SMX therapy?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Monitor sodium and volume status during high-intensity therapy
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Sodium and volume monitoring addresses the described risk.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Diagnose SIADH from the first low sodium value without reviewing volume
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Assumes a mechanism without evaluating volume.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Wait until treatment ends before evaluating symptomatic hyponatremia
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Delays evaluation of a labeled serious symptomatic problem.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Apply the same fluid restriction to every TMP-SMX sodium abnormality
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Ignores the possible salt-losing differential.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: Follow sodium together with symptoms and volume status. The current label requires evaluation and appropriate correction for symptomatic hyponatremia. A fixed diagnosis or universal fluid restriction can overlook a salt-losing presentation.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: Which assessment best evaluates a falling sodium result during TMP-SMX treatment?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Assess sodium trend, volume, dose, renal function, diuretics, intake, and neurologic symptoms
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Covers trajectory, symptoms, renal/drug/intake and volume context.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Use one sodium value and assume the antibiotic proves the mechanism
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: One result and drug identity do not identify the cause.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Review diuretic names but omit sodium trend, intake and volume
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Drug names alone omit critical clinical data.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Review kidney function only and disregard neurologic symptoms
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Renal information alone omits sodium severity and symptoms.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: Use the sodium trajectory and complete dose, renal, medicine, intake, symptom and volume context. One value or one category of data cannot distinguish the relevant mechanisms or determine urgency.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: Which diagnostic error should be avoided when sodium falls during TMP-SMX therapy?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Assuming every low sodium value is SIADH
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Automatic SIADH attribution misses a documented alternative drug-related mechanism.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Reviewing the sodium trajectory and volume status
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Appropriate trajectory/volume assessment.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Considering a trimethoprim-related sodium-losing effect
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Appropriate consideration of a possible drug-related mechanism.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Evaluating symptoms and other sodium-altering medicines
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Appropriate symptom and medication evaluation.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: Automatically labeling every low sodium result SIADH ignores alternative mechanisms. Considering drug-related salt loss, reviewing the trajectory and medicines, and assessing symptoms and volume are appropriate parts of the evaluation.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: Which principle best supports a TMP-SMX fluid and crystalluria plan?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Adequate hydration and renal monitoring help reduce concentrated urinary exposure and crystal risk
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Compatible with book crystalluria/water counseling and label fluid/output and renal follow-up.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: A large fixed fluid load is appropriate regardless of congestion
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Uses a fixed large load without volume context.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: A normal baseline creatinine eliminates the need to assess urine output
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Normal baseline creatinine does not remove the output assessment.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Adequate water intake makes electrolyte follow-up unnecessary
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Water does not remove the labeled electrolyte-monitoring requirement.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: The book identifies crystalluria and advises water; the label specifies adequate fluid intake and urine output. Hydration advice should fit volume and kidney context, and it does not eliminate the need for electrolyte or renal surveillance.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: Which clinical action best applies to TMP-SMX hydration counseling?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Create an individualized fluid plan and avoid automatic overhydration in heart or kidney failure
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Preserves adequate hydration counseling while considering actual patient volume constraints.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Prescribe a universal large fluid volume without assessing congestion
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Indiscriminate loading omits the retained congestion context.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Withhold all fluid automatically from every patient with CKD
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Automatic total avoidance is not individualized adequate hydration.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Replace the potassium and sodium plan with advice to drink more water
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Hydration advice cannot replace electrolyte monitoring.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: Make adequate hydration compatible with the patient's intake, output, kidney reserve and volume constraints. Neither indiscriminate loading nor automatic total fluid avoidance is an individualized plan; water advice cannot replace laboratory follow-up.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: Which assessment best informs TMP-SMX hydration and crystalluria counseling?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Assess intake, urine output, volume status, heart failure, kidney function, route, and dose
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Includes actual intake/output,volume,kidney context and exposure.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Use the tablet name alone and omit volume or kidney assessment
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Product name alone does not assess the patient.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Check reported thirst only and omit urine output and congestion
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Thirst alone omits urine/output and volume information.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Treat a normal initial potassium as proof that any fluid load is suitable
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Potassium alone does not establish fluid tolerability.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: Review actual intake, urine output, volume status, heart failure and kidney function alongside product route and exposure. Tablet identity, thirst alone or potassium alone does not establish a suitable fluid plan.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: Which error should be prevented in TMP-SMX fluid counseling?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Giving a universal large fluid load regardless of congestion
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: A universal large load disregards the volume constraints retained in the lesson.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Checking congestion and urine output before advising fluid intake
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Appropriate congestion/output assessment.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Reconciling the fluid advice with kidney function and prescribed exposure
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Appropriate kidney/exposure reconciliation.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Keeping potassium and sodium follow-up in the treatment plan
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Appropriate continuation of electrolyte surveillance.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: An automatic large fluid load disregards congestion and limited kidney reserve. Checking volume and output, reconciling exposure and maintaining electrolyte surveillance are appropriate safeguards.

questionReviews.stemActuallyRead: A patient with CKD takes lisinopril and spironolactone. TMP-SMX is proposed. What is the most important immediate safety plan?

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Choose an alternative when possible or arrange early potassium and renal monitoring
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: An effective alternative or active potassium/renal follow-up addresses the CKD and combined potassium-raising drugs.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Wait until therapy ends to measure potassium
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Delays follow-up through the course.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Add potassium supplementation
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Adds potassium to the risk stack without an indication.

fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.choice: Double spironolactone
fourChoicesIndividuallyReviewed.judgment: Increases a potassium-raising drug rather than addressing risk.

questionReviews.rationaleActuallyRead: CKD, lisinopril and spironolactone create a strong potassium-retention risk when TMP-SMX is proposed. Review an effective alternative when feasible, or arrange potassium and renal follow-up during treatment with a named reviewer and escalation plan. Recommended antibiotic dosing does not remove the risk. The current label requires action on significant electrolyte or renal abnormalities.

ARB alone with normal kidney function can carry risk but does not match CKD plus the two potassium-raising agents.
